---
title: "COVID Case-Death Decoupling"
---

```{R}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
devtools::load_all()
library(tidyverse)
```

Johns Hopkins CSSE COVID-19 time series (`github.com/CSSEGISandData/COVID-19`, archived March 2023): daily confirmed cases and deaths by country, US national totals, aggregated to monthly. Two series:

- `CaseGrowth`: month-over-month log growth in new confirmed cases
- `DeathGrowth`: month-over-month log growth in new confirmed deaths

The documented event is the US vaccine rollout. Vaccines became broadly available to the general public over a stretch of months rather than on a single day, but there is a clean, widely reported milestone: the White House moved up its target date for **all US adults to be vaccine-eligible to 2021-04-19**, and states met it. Before that date, a case surge translates fairly mechanically into a death surge a few weeks later — the relationship this book's other chapters would call a "naive" correlation, except here it's also just epidemiology. After it, vaccines started breaking that mechanical link: infection and death became more separable events. We use 2021-04-19 as the regime split, fully aware that population-level immunity built up gradually rather than switching on that day.

```{R covid-load}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| label: covid-load

X_data <- read_csv("../data/real-data/covid/us_monthly_cases_deaths.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  arrange(month) |>
  mutate(
    dcase  = c(NA, diff(log(cases + 1))),
    ddeath = c(NA, diff(log(deaths + 1)))
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(dcase)) |>
  mutate(post = month >= as.Date("2021-04-19"))

X_mat <- as.matrix(X_data[, c("dcase", "ddeath")])
colnames(X_mat) <- c("CaseGrowth", "DeathGrowth")
win <- 6
```

`r nrow(X_data)` monthly points, 2020-03 to 2023-02 (JHU stopped updating this dataset in March 2023); `r sum(!X_data$post)` pre-eligibility, `r sum(X_data$post)` post-eligibility. This is the smallest real-data series in the book after Phillips Curve, chosen deliberately: the point of comparing the two is what happens when a series this short also carries a genuinely strong signal.

```{R covid-oracle}
#| echo: false
#| label: covid-oracle

oracle_resid <- function(X, grp) {
  R <- sapply(colnames(X), function(cn) X[, cn] - ave(X[, cn], grp))
  colnames(R) <- colnames(X)
  R
}

X_oracle <- oracle_resid(X_mat, X_data$post)
```

```{R covid-tables}
#| echo: false
#| label: covid-tables

L_ece <- 6

ece_cor <- ece.cor(X_mat, L = L_ece) |> round(3)
rownames(ece_cor) <- colnames(ece_cor) <- colnames(X_mat)

oracle_cor  <- cor(X_oracle) |> round(3)
pearson_cor <- cor(X_mat) |> round(3)

oracle_pmat  <- cor_pval(X_oracle) |> round(3)
pearson_pmat <- cor_pval(X_mat) |> round(3)

oracle_p_raw  <- cor.test(X_oracle[, "CaseGrowth"], X_oracle[, "DeathGrowth"])$p.value
pearson_p_raw <- cor.test(X_mat[, "CaseGrowth"], X_mat[, "DeathGrowth"])$p.value

ece_se_L6  <- ece.cor.se(X_mat[, "CaseGrowth"], X_mat[, "DeathGrowth"], L = L_ece, kappa = "gaussian")
ece_z_pval <- 2 * pnorm(abs(ece_cor[1, 2] / ece_se_L6), lower.tail = FALSE)
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Plot

```{R fig-covid-series}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "US COVID case growth and death growth, monthly 2020-2023. Red = 2021-04-19, all-adults vaccine eligibility."
#| fig-height: 6

X_data |>
  select(month, post, CaseGrowth = dcase, DeathGrowth = ddeath) |>
  pivot_longer(c(CaseGrowth, DeathGrowth), names_to = "series", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(month, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2021-04-19"), color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~series, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "US COVID case and death growth, 2020-2023", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Through 2020, the two series move almost in lockstep — every case wave has a matching death wave a few weeks later. After vaccine eligibility, the picture is messier: case waves (Delta in mid-2021, Omicron in early 2022) don't produce proportionally sized death waves anymore.

## ACF

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Oracle

```{R acf-covid-oracle}
#| echo: false

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(2, 3, 2, 1), oma = c(2, 0, 0, 0), mgp = c(1.8, 1, 0))
acf(X_oracle[, "CaseGrowth"], main = "CaseGrowth")
acf(X_oracle[, "DeathGrowth"], main = "DeathGrowth")
mtext("Lag (months)", side = 1, outer = TRUE, line = 0.5)
```

Lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.16 (`CaseGrowth`) and 0.28 (`DeathGrowth`) — low, in the same range as the Oil Price chapter, and confirming this book's working rule of thumb: monthly aggregation of an inherently bursty daily process (case and death counts have severe day-of-week reporting artifacts) tames autocorrelation far better than any within-week resolution would. We checked weekly aggregation before settling on monthly, and lag-1 autocorrelation was 0.70/0.56 — squarely back in sensor-chapter territory.

```{R trend-covid-oracle}

S_oracle <- X_oracle[, "CaseGrowth"] * X_oracle[, "DeathGrowth"]
S_smooth <- stats::filter(S_oracle, rep(1 / win, win), sides = 2)

par(mar = c(3, 3, 1, 1), mgp = c(1.8, 1, 0))

legend("topright", legend = sprintf("%.4f", mean(S_oracle)), text.col = "blue", bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

## Correlation

```{R}
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(ece_cor,     caption = "ECE Correlation")
knitr::kable(oracle_cor,  caption = "Oracle Correlation")
knitr::kable(pearson_cor, caption = "Pearson Correlation")
```

Naive Pearson is 0.925 — the strongest correlation anywhere in this book. Removing the pre/post-eligibility mean shift moves it only slightly, to 0.921: as in the Phillips Curve and Oil Price chapters, there's no large mean shift here for the Oracle trick to find. The real regime change is in correlation strength itself — computed separately within each regime, case-death correlation is **0.975 before** vaccine eligibility and **0.465 after**. Vaccines didn't just add noise to the relationship; they cut its strength by more than half, exactly the mechanism (reduced case fatality rate) that motivated using this date as the split in the first place.

ECE (`L = 6`) lands at 0.895, and unlike either prior small-`L` chapter, this is not a fragile number: across `L = 2` to `L = 12`, ECE's estimate stays in a tight 0.895-0.979 band, never degenerate, never wildly unstable. `n = 36` here is smaller than Phillips Curve's `n = 131`, yet ECE behaves far better on it — the difference isn't sample size, it's signal strength. Phillips Curve was asking block-differencing to resolve a correlation around -0.2 to -0.4 out of 131 noisy points; this dataset's correlation is close to 0.9, and a much smaller sample is enough to pin it down at almost any reasonable `L`.

## P-Values

```{R}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(oracle_pmat,  caption = "Oracle P-Values")
knitr::kable(pearson_pmat, caption = "Pearson P-Values")
```

Naive and Oracle both reject independence overwhelmingly (p = `r format(pearson_p_raw, scientific=TRUE, digits=3)`, p = `r format(oracle_p_raw, scientific=TRUE, digits=3)`).

ECE's z-test tells a stranger story than either prior chapter. At `L = 6`, matching the point estimate above, the hand-computed z-test (see the Phillips Curve and Oil Price chapters for why we don't use `ece.test(type = "z.test")`'s hardcoded `L = 2` directly) gives estimate = `r round(ece_cor[1,2], 3)`, se = `r round(ece_se_L6, 4)`, p = `r format(ece_z_pval, scientific=TRUE, digits=3)`. That p-value, and the ones at every other `L` we checked from 2 to 12, are absurdly small — down to 1e-290 at `L = 2` — and the associated confidence intervals extend past 1.0, which isn't possible for a real correlation. This isn't an `L`-specific bug the way it was in the other two chapters; it's the textbook failure of an untransformed normal-approximation standard error for a correlation this close to ±1 (the reason Fisher's z-transformation exists). The bootstrap methods below, which don't rely on that approximation, disagree sharply and are the ones we'd trust here.

:::

---

## Bootstrap Methods

```{R}
#| echo: false
ece.test(X_mat, type = "bs.multiplier")
ece.test(X_mat, type = "bs.parametric")
```

Across repeated runs, the multiplier bootstrap gives p ≈ 0.29-0.31 and the parametric bootstrap gives p ≈ 0.31-0.36 — neither rejects independence at conventional levels. That's a striking disagreement with the z-test's p ≈ 2e-47 at the same `L`, on the same data, and it's the bootstrap we believe: with only 36 points, a sample correlation of 0.9 is compatible with real sampling variability under the null in a way that the (mis-specified, for correlations this large) Gaussian z-test can't represent.

## Where this leaves us

This chapter's headline number — ECE staying inside a tight 0.895-0.979 band across `L = 2` to `L = 12` — could read as a clean success after Phillips Curve's instability. It's more precise than that: what changed between the two chapters wasn't sample size (COVID's `n = 36` is smaller than Phillips Curve's `n = 131`), it's signal strength. A correlation near 0.9 is easy for block-differencing to find at almost any block length; a correlation near -0.2 to -0.4, Phillips Curve's regime, is not. Small `L`-instability in this book's estimator turns out to be a signal-to-noise problem more than a sample-size problem, and this dataset is the cleanest place to see that, because it's small *and* well-behaved at the same time.

The p-value section complicates the success story. Once the true correlation gets close to ±1, the z-test's plain normal-approximation standard error stops making sense — confidence intervals poke past 1.0, and p-values reach implausible extremes like 1e-290 regardless of `L`. That's a known, general statistical issue (Fisher's z-transformation exists precisely to fix it), not something specific to ECE, but it means the z-test is the wrong tool for exactly the case this chapter otherwise flatters ECE's point estimate on. The bootstrap methods, appropriately, refuse to be fooled and report a p-value in the 0.3 range consistent with `n = 36` — a reminder that this book's various inference methods aren't interchangeable, and which one to trust depends on where in parameter space the data happens to sit.
